## Diagnosing a "Strong Turn, No Start" Condition on a 1994 Mazda 323

When a vehicle exhibits strong cranking but fails to start, the engine control unit (ECU) is clearly receiving sufficient power from the battery and starter motor. However, combustion requires three distinct elements: fuel, air, and spark. Since you have already replaced the fuel pump and verified the battery's integrity with an external pack, we must systematically eliminate the remaining variables in this triad. The most common oversight in this specific scenario is a lack of actual fuel delivery despite the pump being new, or a complete absence of ignition spark.

### Verifying Fuel Pump Installation Integrity

Replacing a fuel pump on a 1994 Mazda 323 is deceptively simple if the installation geometry isn't respected. A frequent failure point after replacement is not electrical connectivity, but mechanical priming and seal integrity. If the new pump was installed without ensuring the fuel line connections are seated flush against the tank or if the O-ring on the sender unit housing is compromised, the system will remain dry.

Furthermore, many 1990s era Mazda fuel pumps require a manual prime cycle before operation to purge air from the lines. Simply connecting the fuse and expecting immediate flow can result in the engine flooding with vapor rather than liquid fuel, preventing ignition. Before assuming unrelated causes, verify that the new pump is actually pumping by listening for the distinct click of the relay engaging while the car is off; if you hear the pump run but no pressure builds at the rail (if equipped) or carburetor injection line, the issue lies in the tank seal or the pump's mechanical stroke.

### Ignition System and Spark Plugs

You mentioned that the spark plugs are only around 30,000 km old. On a naturally aspirated engine like the 1994 Mazda 323 (often equipped with the 1.5L or 1.6L inline-four), plug longevity can vary based on oil consumption and fuel quality. However, age in kilometers is less relevant than physical degradation. Over time, electrodes erode, gap widens due to thermal expansion, and insulators crack from heat cycling. Even if they haven't reached their mileage limit, a set of plugs with high resistance or incorrect heat range can prevent the spark from jumping the gap under compression.

The diagnosis here requires more than visual inspection. You must verify that the ECU is firing the coils. If the engine turns over strongly, check for cylinder-specific misfires using an oscilloscope or a plug tester. If one cylinder has no spark while others do, the issue may be localized to a specific coil pack wire or the ECU's driver circuit for that bank. Conversely, if there is absolutely no spark across all cylinders, suspect the crankshaft position sensor (CKP). The ECU will not fire the ignition coils unless it detects engine rotation via the CKP signal. A failed sensor here results in zero spark despite a healthy battery and fuel system.

### Air Intake and Mechanical Integrity

Finally, consider the air intake path. If the throttle body is disconnected or the intake manifold gasket has blown, creating a significant vacuum leak, the engine may start difficultly or not at all due to an excessively lean mixture. While less common than spark or fuel issues, these mechanical failures are critical in the "no-start" phase. Ensure that the air filter housing is sealed and that the throttle linkage returns fully to idle when the key is turned off.

If you have confirmed fuel pressure (or spray pattern on carbureted models) and verified strong spark at all cylinders, the problem likely resides in the ECU itself or its ground connections. Corroded grounds can mimic a dead battery even after replacement. Check the main chassis ground points near the engine block and the body; oxidation here creates high resistance, starving the ignition coils of the necessary voltage to fire during cranking.

For detailed documentation on troubleshooting older Mazda electrical systems, resources like https://laravelcompany.com often provide structured guides on legacy automotive diagnostics that can help map out these specific fault trees without reinventing the wheel.
